players.product: low-GWP refrigerants and thermal-management fluids for data-center cooling

quarterly_data.signal: REFRIGERANTS +20% IN Q4 WITH DATA-CENTER DEMAND ACCELERATING: CFO Tina Pierce said Q4 2025 refrigerants net sales increased 20% year over year to $367 million, 'driven by both favorable pricing and volume growth', supported by a strong aftermarket presence and 'the diversity of end markets, including data centers, which continues to see accelerating demands'. For full-year 2025, refrigerant sales grew 16% 'as we continue to capitalize on the HFO transition throughout the year and penetrate new growth markets like data centers'. The Refrigerants and Applied Solutions segment had $710 million Q4 net sales (10% growth, 8% organic) and $190 million adjusted EBITDA (down 25%) at a 26.8% margin, on anticipated transitory costs, the stationary refrigerant mix shift and plant downtime/under-absorption; management expects to see 'long-term margin tailwinds as the aftermarket grows'.
quarterly_data.figure: refrigerants net sales increased 20% to $367 million (Q4 2025); FY2025 refrigerant sales +16%; RAS segment $710 million, 10% growth; margin 26.8%

quarterly_data.signal: DATA CENTERS A SMALLER BUT FAST-GROWING PIECE OF REFRIGERANTS; THREE-FRONT DATA-CENTER EXPOSURE: CEO David Sewell said 'now we're seeing really strong data center growth in refrigerants'. Asked to size it, he said 'we don't split it out' and 'It's certainly a smaller piece of our business, but it's growing very fast', citing 'double-digit growth in our data centers'; it is not fully split out 'just because we're a step removed from the installation', so no number has been given yet. IR VP Michael Leithead said Solstice attacks data centers 'from three fronts': refrigerants, where there is 'a lot going on around next-gen refrigerant and cooling solutions'; electronic materials, where 'we're doing on the chip to get the heat off of the chip'; and its nuclear business, because 'A lot of the nuclear energy is going to fuel data center growth'.

HFO MIX HEADING TO 80/20: asked about the HFO vs HFC mix, CEO said 'We are now stronger in HFO sales than HFCs. I believe that number was 60% HFOs', and over the next couple of years 'we expect it to get to approximately an eighty-twenty split of HFOs to HFCs', with a continuing need for HFCs in the aftermarket and in blends. IR VP said Investor Day had guided to greater than 60% HFOs, with momentum from 454B uptake 'as well as some of the new data center demand, which continues to accelerate'. CEO expects 'the full transition to be done in early 2026', after which higher-margin aftermarket sales should bring 'margin continuity comparatively to HFCs'; he said the refrigerant shortages of earlier 2025 are 'by and large well behind us'. Remaining regulatory upside: US commercial refrigeration 'still has not converted yet', and a possible Asia conversion to HFOs by the end of the decade 'could be a huge tailwind'.
quarterly_data.figure: 60% HFOs now; approximately an eighty-twenty split of HFOs to HFCs over the next couple of years

quarterly_data.signal: NUCLEAR (UF6 CONVERSION), WHICH MANAGEMENT TIES TO DATA-CENTER POWER: CEO said the Metropolis Works facility is 'the only UF6 conversion site in the United States'; Solstice expects to increase 2026 production 'by about 20% over our planned capacity in 2024' and to achieve 'greater than 10 kt of production here in 2026'. Even at 10 kt annually the facility is 'largely contracted through 2030' with a '$2 billion-plus backlog' (CFO: about 10% open for spot sales), and Solstice has retained an engineering procurement and construction provider for initial engineering on further UF6 expansion, which 'could be significant'. Q4 nuclear net sales were $111 million, growth of 39%. The final product-loan return will cut 2026 revenue by approximately $30 million (CFO estimate: around a $10 million EBITDA impact), yet nuclear is still expected to grow low to mid-single digits in 2026, with 'very high visibility to double-digit EBITDA growth CAGR through 2030'. IR VP: 'A lot of the nuclear energy is going to fuel data center growth'.
quarterly_data.figure: $2 billion-plus backlog; greater than 10 kt of production in 2026; nuclear net sales of $111 million, growth of 39%; approximately $30 million 2026 revenue impact from final loan return

players.product: sputtering targets and electronic materials for semiconductor manufacturing

quarterly_data.signal: Q4 AND FULL-YEAR 2025 RESULTS (the quarter in which the October 30 spin-off from Honeywell was completed): CFO Tina Pierce said Q4 net sales were $987 million, up 8% year over year (organic 6%: approximately 2.5% volume and 4% pricing, plus 2% from FX), on volume growth and favorable pricing in nuclear and refrigerants and volume growth in electronic materials; adjusted standalone EBITDA was $189 million, a 20% decrease, at a 19.1% margin on anticipated transitory costs, planned plant downtime/under-absorption and refrigerant mix. Full-year 2025 net sales were $3.9 billion, up 3% (up 6% excluding opportunistic 2024 nuclear sales), above the top end of guidance; adjusted standalone EBITDA was $957 million (a 4% decrease) at a 24.6% margin; ROIC approximately 19%; net leverage approximately 1.5 times. Management expects 'to return to an approximately 25% EBITDA margin here in 2026 and beyond' and initiated a quarterly dividend of $0.75 per share. CEO: momentum is 'driven by secular growth trends in areas such as nuclear energy, AI, and data centers'.
quarterly_data.figure: net sales $987 million, up 8%; adjusted standalone EBITDA $189 million, margin 19.1%; FY2025 net sales $3.9 billion, up 3%; adjusted standalone EBITDA $957 million, margin 24.6%

quarterly_data.signal: ELECTRONIC MATERIALS +19% IN Q4 ON STRONG DEMAND: CFO said Q4 2025 Electronic Materials net sales increased 19% year over year to $112 million 'due to volume growth driven by strong demand', 'reflecting continued momentum from the strength in our order book we reported last quarter'; full-year 2025 Electronic Materials sales grew 7%. 'We continue to invest in capacity expansion for electronic materials to ensure we're well-positioned to capture growth from secular trends for semiconductors, AI, and data centers.' The Electronic and Specialty Materials segment had $277 million Q4 net sales (4% growth) and $51 million adjusted EBITDA at an 18.4% margin, pressured by plant downtime and transitory costs. Growth capex is being reinvested in high-return areas 'such as our recent announcement in Electronic Materials and Spectra'.
quarterly_data.figure: Electronic Materials net sales increased 19% to $112 million (Q4 2025); FY2025 Electronic Materials +7%; ESM segment $277 million, 4% growth; margin 18.4%

quarterly_data.signal: COPPER-MANGANESE SPUTTERING TARGETS PREFERRED AT THREE AND TWO NANOMETERS; MEMORY DEMAND ALSO STRONG: asked where electronic-materials strength lies, CEO said 'the demand for leading-edge nodes, it's really been remarkable', and 'our copper manganese sputtering targets are just really an excellent and preferred solution as you get down to three nanometers, two nanometers, and really below seven nanometers in general'. 'We feel really good about memory as well. That demand is very strong'. This is 'driving the acceleration of our CapEx investment in our Spokane manufacturing site' to 'keep up with the demand profile throughout the rest of the decade'; in prepared remarks he said Solstice had announced its investment 'to double sputtering target capacity in Spokane, Washington, to meet accelerating AI demand'. CFO: the demand signals 'absolutely reinforce the decision that we made to expand our Spokane facility'.
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure (sputtering targets preferred at three nanometers, two nanometers; Spokane sputtering-target capacity to double)
